title: Four random positive-catch nights per month added 167% to mean squared annual catch differences at seven UK moth traps
abstract: We tested how night selection changes annual moth catch differences relative to the full recorded schedule. We used single-night UK Environmental Change Network samples, equal monthly means of positive-night count proportions, and 34 consecutive-year pairs at seven traps in 1993-2015. Simple random sampling of four positive nights per month added 167% to the mean squared annual difference. Thus 62.5% of the expected sparse-sample difference came from selection, with a conditional whole-site bootstrap range of 56.2-66.8%. Equal-presence vectors and stricter coverage kept this result. The point estimate inflated external thermal-score differences slightly more than total composition differences, but the paired site range allowed either direction. Sparse sampling did not establish a loss of thermal alignment. A standard finite-population variance identity gives an exact expected excess and an unbiased correction. Exhaustive examples and 4,000 real-data draws checked the correction. This is a calibration against recorded catches, not an estimate of biological turnover or the thermal-tracking gap. Positive-night conditioning, seven traps, capture effects, selected coverage and external-score bias limit interpretation. Code, aggregate results, a figure, source hashes and reproduction instructions are included. External records remain outside the package.
